utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Harvey?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. May I introduce Ms. Samie Blasingame, who is from Long Beach University, California, California State University Long Beach, I should say, where she has a bachelor's in international relations. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harvey. Yes, Ms. Edgerton, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And just one brief note to follow up on something from yesterday, Your Honours, that Dr. Karadzic raised regarding P4484, which is the recorded conversation between he and General Zivanovic. He asked at transcript page 42518 about the date, and I undertook to update everyone as to the evidence of the conversation or regarding the conversation in that regard. And I'd like to refer Dr. Karadzic to transcript pages 27485 to 27488, and in fact, at transcript -- at transcript page 27727, Dr. Karadzic himself accepted the date of the conversation as being the 8th of July and he must have forgot about that. So this is just to answer his query of yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Whose evidence was it about?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, one quick thing from yesterday -- Zivanovic, pardon me, Zametica. One quick thing from yesterday, the document we left off discussing, you had never seen that before I showed it to you yesterday; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You will have to remind which document we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, if you don't remember the very last document we discussed yesterday, I'll simply move on because it was just a brief query, and deal with another topic. You knew, Mr. Zametica, on 13 July 1995, that Bosnian Serb forces in Srebrenica had prisoners; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the date, but yes, because the military action was successful. The Serb forces had entered the town. It would be reasonable to assume that there were some prisoners, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. You knew they had prisoners actually in Potocari; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You knew the prisoners were men?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know whether they were in Potocari. I mean Potocari meant nothing to me at the time. I didn't know the geography of the area, I've never been there in my life. Whether I knew that they were men, I assumed they were men, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You assumed that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Because actually, what you said in a BBC radio interview on July 13, 1995, was exactly that. You were told that the Bosnian Serbs were arresting all Muslim men in Srebrenica in a search for war criminals and you said -- and you didn't deny that. You said, "We are separating the men from women, children and the elderly."

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What did I not deny? I'm sorry, I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Could we have the reference for that, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, sure, we can have a look at it. 65 ter number 25328, please. And it's a transcript of a BBC 4 radio programme at 6.29 p.m. on the 13th of July, 1995. And it was on the subject of events at Srebrenica. If we he can go over to page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Zametica, the interviewer pointed out to you it's not the UN who are separating men from their families, putting them on buses and driving them from their homes. And you said: We are separating the men from women and children -- Mr. Zametica, let me finish my question. You said: We are separating the men from women, children and elderly, for a very good reason, and it was to question some of those men. And then if you go further down the page, the interviewer said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let him read it. Let him read it and why don't you ask a question after he finished his reading.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like you to --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Only because I'm conscious of my time, Your Honour, but, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, I would like to read the whole page. At the moment I only see two paragraphs. And if we can enlarge the whole thing, please, so I can have a close look at the document. Thank you. I've read the page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, since you've read the page, I'll direct you to the last question from the interviewer, the last statement from the interviewer. The interviewer put to you that's why all the males aged 16 and upwards, including old men, are being taken from their families. And if you go over to the top of the next page, you'll see you didn't deny it.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, where does -- where does the interviewer say age 16? Can we have that again? That's what he says.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I can finish my question. If we go over to the top of the next page, you didn't deny it. Can we go back to the top the next page? Your answer was: We wish to carry out a thorough investigation. So, Mr. Zametica, it's more than just a reasonable assumption that you had prisoners, and it's more than just an assumption that you had men. You knew, on the 13th of July, 1995, that Bosnian Serb forces had prisoners in Srebrenica; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. This is extraordinary. If we go back to the previous page, please, where the interviewer says, so that is why all the males aged from 16 upwards, and he has another few sentences, and I then reply or follow that up with whatever I say on the next page, it does not follow at all, there is no logic in this. Perhaps I just failed to comment on -- maybe I didn't hear him properly. This is not -- this is -- he probably called me on the telephone, he called me from London. Maybe I didn't hear the number 16. But, I mean, to extrapolate from this that, you know, I knew there were men aged from 16 upwards is, I think, you know, something that I would absolutely reject. It just doesn't follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You knew there were prisoners?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew there were prisoners but --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You knew that the men --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know the age of the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You knew that the men were being separated from the women and children --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have this transcript as a Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6475, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, knowing that there were prisoners who were being separated, you knew that they should be registered; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: By "registered," you mean what, if I may ask?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Registered at their place of detention, registered by the ICRC. You knew that; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know the procedure of how you treat prisoners of war. I mean, I had never taken a prisoner of war myself. I had no direct experience of that. I was a civilian. So if you ask me: Did you know, Mr. Zametica, about the exact procedure of the bureaucratic side of it, how you treat a war prisoner, my answer is no, I have no idea. I presume the army knew.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You knew that there should be a massive exchange at some point; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I know there should be a massive exchange at some point? You say "massive"?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Zametica, do I need to repeat every question to you? Was I unclear?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you were unclear because you used the term "massive" which implies that I knew the number of prisoners. I had no idea about the number of prisoners. So to imply that you knew there should be a massive exchange of prisoners, is simply unfair because I had no idea about the number of prisoners. I didn't know whether there was one, two or 2.000. I had no idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one told me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Zametica, it's clear from this interview that we just looked at that you anticipated a release of prisoners eventually. Now, Mr. Zametica, you knew that there should be an exchange; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prisoner exchanges were common practice during the war, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So where are the personal records of these prisoners, Mr. Zametica?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Where, Mr. Zametica, are their records of detention?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have absolutely no idea. That was not my job to deal with records or follow-up this sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Where, then -- do you know where their records of interrogation are?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is absolutely beyond my sphere of responsibility or activity. Absolutely no idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could please have this interview that we just looked at, 65 ter number 25328, back up on the screen, please? If we could go back over now to page 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Zametica, here in this further transcript, you talked about the investigations that these prisoners were going to be undergoing. You talked about those investigations being a rapid exercise. You told the world that these people were going to be processed and released in a matter of weeks. And you now say you have no idea how that was supposed to come about; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I mean, just because one doesn't know the bureaucratic side of it doesn't mean to say that you have no idea, at least the implication you just made. And what is it that should have made me think there wouldn't be an exchange of prisoners? This was common practice. It was in our interests, as well as the interests of the Muslim side, to exchange prisoners. We were doing it all the time. I was fully expecting a prisoner exchange, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right, then. So where are they? Where are the prisoners? Where was the exchange?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We talked about this yesterday. I said there was a massacre.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Zametica, just to stay with the events at Potocari for a moment, and the separations you talked about in this interview. You know, Svetozar Kosoric, who was the chief intelligence officer at the Drina Corps came to testify as a Defence witness for Dr. Karadzic and --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, what was his surname, please, again.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Kosoric.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kosoric.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And he was in Potocari on the 12th of July and he stayed in Bratunac that night, and when he came to testify he said he knew nothing about the separations. And that's at transcript page 38698 and further 38705 to 38707. And Zvonko Bajagic, who was in the Drina Corps's logistics unit - whose witness statement, Your Honours, is at 1D09611 - also came to give evidence for Dr. Karadzic's Defence and he went through Potocari on the 13th of July, en route to Srebrenica, and he saw buses at Potocari being loaded with Muslims. And he says, in this statement that I just cited to, that he didn't see any men getting separated from the women and children. So as regards the separations, it looks like you, at Pale, are better informed than the military on the ground; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When we are talking about the separation, and when Bajagic says he didn't see anything, we don't know which day he's talking about, what hour, which location. This other person you mentioned earlier on, Kosoric, again, I think same applies. Are you saying that children and women were not separated from the men?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Zametica, you keep asking me questions, but this isn't a conversation. So if you could stop that, you'll be done here much sooner this morning. Now, moving on in time, on the 15th of July, 1995, you knew, Mr. Zametica, that you had even more prisoners in Srebrenica; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm waiting for your follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Zametica, this is a "yes" or "no" question. By 15 July 1995, you knew you had even more prisoners; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not a "yes" or "no" question. This is a question of 20 years ago or almost 20 years ago. That is why I said I'm waiting for your follow-up question because I don't know what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't understand your answer, Mr. Zametica. Until just now, we talked about 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And she said -- Ms. Edgerton moved to -- moved on to 15th and then asked whether you knew that there were more prisoners. The answer can be either "yes" or "no," or you didn't know, you don't remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for this clarification. In that case, my answer is: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you didn't know that the VRS Main Staff had reported to the president on the 15th of July, 1995, that the main body of the Drina Corps was engaged in defence, whereas the Milici and Bratunac Brigades as well as the Skelani Independent Battalion are securing the terrain and receiving a large number of fighters who were surrendering to them? You didn't know that, did you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember. I really cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The reference to that, by the way, is P4457.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, Mr. Zametica, Dr. Karadzic showed you D3931, which was your press statement dated 17 July 1995. And it was -- or one of your press statements. It was carried by AFP, and in that, you said: "Allegations of torture, murder, rape and deportation of Muslim civilians are made repeatedly without independent verification. The truth is that none of these things have happened." And you told the Court you thought everything was being done in accordance with all the conventions. And that was at temporary transcript page 57. And that was because you said Koljevic told you Mladic had said he let the Red Cross into Srebrenica and because of the agreement. This all formed a picture in your mind. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right. So that was enough, then, the evidence that Koljevic told Mladic he'd let the Red Cross into Srebrenica, and the agreement, that was enough for you to credibly -- pardon me, enough for you to credibly deny the allegations of torture, murder, rape, and deportation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not saying that was enough. But almost 20 years after the event, those are the two factors that I do remember or had access to in documents to see. There may have been, and there probably were, other factors, other information, which would have strengthened me in my belief that everything had gone in accordance with the conventions.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Let's talk about one of those two factors. Let's talk about the agreement. That agreement, Mr. Zametica, was pure propaganda. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The definition of propaganda is lie or spreading of lies. So are you saying that the agreement that was signed by the -- among other people, the Muslim civilian representative in Srebrenica, as well as the UN representative, that they were party to spreading lies? Is that what you're saying? I'm not sure what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh. Mr. Zametica, I'm saying that that agreement was a fake that was created by you and Dr. Karadzic and other people to avert blame for the forcible transfer of civilians from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Zametica, what was true about the situation for civilians in Potocari was that there were thousands there, they were homeless, they had no accommodation, they were unable to move, and they had no real choice about whether they were going to stay or go. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the factors that I remember now which contributed to this conviction on my part that everything had been going in accordance with rules, regulations, conventions, I now remember that I also saw on our TV footage from Srebrenica showing General Mladic in town and showing him in front of a crowd of Muslim civilians, mostly elderly men and women and children, and he was, if I remember correctly, speaking to some of them, and I think the footage also showed some of those civilians being -- embarking on the buses, and going somewhere. So I presumed everything was -- that the civilian population was being evacuated, and I subsequently found out -- I think it was they were being evacuated through, I believe, Tuzla. So that is the memory I have of those days.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My question to you, Mr. Zametica, was specifically related to the situation for civilians in Potocari on the 12th and 13th and 14th of July, 1994, and the days that immediately followed. There were thousands of people there, they were homeless, they had no accommodation, they were unable to come and go, they had no food, they had no infrastructure, and no means of survival. Yes or no? Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is precisely why they were being evacuated to the place -- I think they were -- I can't remember, but I seem to vaguely remember that they were asked whether they wanted to stay or not, at least some of those civilians were. But my understanding is that those -- that a lot of the Muslims, especially Muslim men, feared local revenge if they stayed on in Srebrenica after Srebrenica was captured by the Bosnian Serb forces, and the majority decided to leave because -- precisely because they feared Serb revenge. And they feared local Serb revenge because of the events taking place in the period before the capture of Srebrenica by the Bosnian Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Zametica --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, wait a minute. I -- this is very important. Srebrenica was -- and the area around Srebrenica --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Zametica, I'm not asking you about the period before the capture. I'm asking you about the situation for civilians at the time. And your answer was quite lengthy, but I take it you agreed with my accounting of the conditions of life for those civilians.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, life for those civilians could not have been a bed of roses. I certainly agree with that. I'm not pretending that civilian population caught in the middle of a war, of a conflict, has it easy. That is precisely why the evacuation was being organised and, as far as I knew, was being carried -- had been carried out.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right. Now, just in regard to this agreement that I've put to you was propaganda, I'd like to draw your attention to -- or bring you back to somebody who Dr. Karadzic prompted you about yesterday, and that's Mr. Deronjic. Now -- and you recalled that you were aware of Mr. Deronjic in response to Dr. Karadzic's prompt. Now, Mr. Zametica, Mr. Deronjic gave a signed statement to the Office of the Prosecutor saying that this agreement that we are talking about was his idea because the killings at Srebrenica had already been reported and Dr. Karadzic approved having the document made. And you, yesterday, said you hadn't personally met him. And even though you may not have personally met him, he also said that you even joined into the discussion about that document because you could use it to show the world that you did the evacuation properly. That's actually how the document was created, how that agreement was made. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly do not remember anything of the kind. Can I please see the document in question that Mr. Deronjic signed?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 65 ter number 22299. And we can go over to paragraph 224 which is at page 67, I think, in English, and 66 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you see Mr. Deronjic's signature in front of you on the cover page of the B/C/S version of that statement. And by the way, the reference to the evidence I've just referred to is also found at paragraphs 221, which we do not see displayed in front of us at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I just --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we can go to paragraph 224, which is the third full paragraph on the right-hand side of the screen, you see that Mr. Deronjic faxed the document to Dr. Karadzic, and you spent a long time discussing it, and you, Mr. Zametica, also joined the conversation.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a technical point, Madam Prosecutor. If you keep talking, I cannot concentrate on reading. So either you talk and I listen to you or you let me concentrate on reading because I would like to read this document. But before I start reading it I would like to know the date of this meeting with Mr. Deronjic. Do we have that? The date?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Zametica, as I told you, this is not a conversation. Read the paragraphs I've referred you to, please, and then I'll have a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not in the least interested in conversing with you. I'm merely concerned to establish the date of this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Why is that, Mr. Zametica? Because you've just said you didn't remember it.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Apparently there was a meeting. I don't -- I certainly don't remember it. But if there was a meeting, I would like to know its date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we are spending more time -- why don't we show him the previous paragraphs where he started talking about this topic?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course. It begins at paragraph 221.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we collapse the B/C/S for the moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I've read the page. Can we please have the following one? I have read this.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If you've read it, then, Mr. Zametica, you would also see at paragraph 226 that Mr. Deronjic also says: "I would like to say that Karadzic and Zametica and myself and other people knew that there were killings and liquidations which is, of course, not discussed in the document." So, Mr. Zametica, not only is the agreement that we are talking about a piece of international propaganda designed to manipulate international reaction and avert blame for the forced transfer of civilians from Srebrenica, you knew about the killings and liquidations; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely incorrect. This is what I have to say on this particular subject. I'm 99 per cent sure that I have not ever met someone called Mr. Deronjic in my life. Certainly not during the war, maybe in passing sometime after the -- but I certainly do not remember a face, and I have a very good memory. So, I'm almost certain that I've never in my life encountered or seen or even -- let alone talked to this man. Now, let's go to his statement. You know, my first impression when I was reading this was -- the first impression was one of total incredulity and when I started thinking about the contents of this statement, in particular paragraph 226, where he says: "I would like to say that Karadzic and Zametica and myself and other people knew," repeat knew, "that there were killings and liquidations which, of course, is not discussed by this document," I can only say this man had some kind of problem with The Hague Tribunal. He was -- he had some kind of deal or agreement with this Tribunal or the investigators, and he had agreed to sign a fabrication, a lie. So this I categorically say is a total fabrication.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Zametica, in that same paragraph that you've just referred to, Mr. Deronjic says, referring to the agreement, that the agreement we have been discussing doesn't correspond with the truth or reality of events in July 1995. The conditions of the evacuation from Potocari, the situation in Potocari, and the broader area were such that they were not favourable for the population to remain there. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Why would then the UN representative sign the agreement?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have these two pages, Your Honours, as a Prosecution exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. This is a way to -- well, first of all, what Mr. Deronjic said is not evidence. Mr. Zametica's comments are the evidence. And you've already rejected the admission of Mr. Deronjic's statements when they were -- Prosecution attempted to admit them under Rule 92 quater. So I don't believe that they could do through the back door what you've already denied them doing through the front door.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You would still object to the admitting of this document if the Chamber is minded to admit it only for the purpose of the context of this witness? Because it was not read out to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I would. I think what the -- the sections of the document that the witness has commented on have been read out to him and he's given his evidence. I don't think there is any need for any part of the statement to be admitted. But if Ms. Edgerton thinks there is something in the statement that she would like elicit his comment from, she is free to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to add anything, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was simply tendering it and limiting it to those pages that we discussed so that the Chamber and the parties can fully understand Mr. Zametica's position on the evidence and nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So not for the truth of the content of those passages?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For that purpose only, we will admit those two pages.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6476, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just your indulgence for a moment while I find something in the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Zametica, you said, when I put to you what Mr. Deronjic said about the conditions of the evacuation in Potocari, your response was, then: Why would the UN representative, then, sign the agreement? Well, Mr. Deronjic, Lieutenant-Colonel Franken, the UN representative whose name is on that agreement, actually confirmed that the agreement was executed under duress and that it's a fabrication. He gave evidence, and has given evidence repeatedly in front of Chambers of this Tribunal, that this document and particularly the part of the agreement that says that the population can remain in the enclave or evacuate is nonsense because they didn't have a realistic opportunity to stay or to move in any direction. They didn't have a choice. Staying in a small area with no means to survive, controlled by the Serbs, being afraid and lethargic as they were, that is not a choice. It was ordered that they should go to the Kladanj area. That was a decision by the representatives but an order -- pardon me, it was not a decision by the representatives but an order of Mladic to go to the area of Kladanj. And that's at P4175, paragraph 105. He also said at paragraph 106: "I did not have any control about what happened." So, Mr. Zametica, the UN individual who signed the agreement actually corroborates what Mr. Deronjic has been saying, corroborates what I've been putting to you, that this agreement is a fake, and it was created to manipulate international reaction. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not the case. Having read Mr. -- parts of Mr. Deronjic's statement, I feel so revolted by it that I thought to myself I'm not going to make any further comments on it because the man is clearly not credible. What he alleges here did not take place. I did not say that I knew there were killings or liquidations. This -- this is a -- this is a total and utter fabrication made under duress, I imagine. And so any of your questions associated with the statement by Mr. Deronjic, I must treat with, well -- I wish -- I wish to say that anything associated with Mr. Deronjic's statement, questions from you connected with his statement, I will treat as very, very, very suspect because the document itself is not suspect, I was going to say "suspect," it's a total lie.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I was asking you --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I'm revolted by it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I was asking you about the evidence of Lieutenant-Colonel Franken, the UN representative who signed the agreement.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know nothing about the evidence given by this Lieutenant-Colonel or whatever his rank was. I would like to see it, but presumably we don't have the time. I'm aware of the time factor. I have no idea what he stated subsequent to the event. All I know in general terms is that the Dutch Battalion there in Srebrenica did not exactly acquit itself in a glorious way in performing its UN duties. Now, perhaps this officer, who signed that statement, felt ashamed or wanted to -- wanted to repaint history or his own role, I have no idea. I do not wish to speculate. But anything associated with this particular statement by Mr. Deronjic is, I think, scandalous.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Zametica, in 1995, you used and abused the fact that Lieutenant-Colonel Franken's name was on that agreement. You issued statements to the effect that UNPROFOR would back you up about the propriety of that evacuation, and I'll read you one of them. It's from P6410, and it's a statement you made on the 17th of July, 1995, to Banja Luka Srpska Televizija. You said that: "Over the past few days, the international media, aided by the Muslim authorities, have engaged in violent propaganda, unrealistically reporting on events relating to the situation in Srebrenica. The accusations concerning alleged torture, killing, rape, and deportation of Muslim civilians are being repeated without any independent verification. The truth is that none of these accusations has a firm basis. UNPROFOR has been on the ground in Srebrenica the entire time and can confirm the fact that the Muslim civilian population was treated well by the Serbs." Mr. Zametica, that's not true, is it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was true, as far as I knew at the time, and I think we've been through this already. Now, I wish to comment on your assertion which you made at the beginning of this little speech you've just made, that I "used and abused the statement made by" -- I forget the Dutch man's name. I did not use and abuse the statement he signed. He did sign that statement. You will not disagree with that. But you would argue that, and you have argued, that he signed it, as you put it, under duress. Can you please tell me under what duress he was when he signed this statement? Was a gun held at him? Was a gun being pointed at him?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Zametica, it's not for you to ask me questions here, with respect. My question to you was with regard to your assertion that UNPROFOR can confirm the fact that the Muslim civilian population was treated well by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, and it did confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's not true. They were not.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but they did. You just agreed with me that he signed the statement. I was not to know -- I mean, it is -- theoretically it's possible that he signed it under duress, yes. I admit theoretically that is possible. But how was I to know that? If, indeed it had been signed under duress? Are you saying to me that over there in Pale, I was supposed to know what was happening in some, I don't know, tent or house in Srebrenica, in a meeting between the Serb forces, Muslim civilians from Srebrenica, and the UN representative? I had no idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So when you said that UNPROFOR can confirm the fact that the Muslim civilian population was treated well by the Serbs, you had actually no idea. That's a lie, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I admire your persistence but, I mean, we are not getting very far here. I think I've explained my position very clearly and I think you understand it, but you keep pushing this, so, you know, carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right, I will, Mr. Zametica. Your job for Dr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask the Prosecution to inform us when was the first time that Franken said that this was under duress? Was that immediately on his return? When? When was that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it's an improper intervention at the moment. You can raise it in your re-examination. Shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You've explained your job for Dr. Karadzic in detail and how one of the aspects of your work was foreign affairs and your job was to stay on top of the international media. Fair?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fair enough, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So it would be normal in the context of your work, and probably as a former resident of the UK, that you would follow the British press. Fair?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, fair.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So on the 17th of July, 1995, you would have seen or been aware that "The Independent" published an article on its front page entitled: "Bodies pile up in horror in Srebrenica"? Because that's your job.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily. The -- in those days, we did not have the internet. Therefore, information, press, was not instantly available the way it is today. So I can't particularly remember that -- that article you've just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, that article was based on, Mr. Zametica, five or six hours of footage that the author and a colleague watched at Studio B's offices in Belgrade, and parts of this film were used in a documentary broadcast by Studio B on the 15th of July, and, in fact, you've already referred to having seen some of that film in your testimony just a few minutes ago. And the tape was from the area of Srebrenica on 13 and 14 July 1995, recorded by a Serbian journalist called Zoran Petrovic-Pirocanac. And among other things, it showed piles of bodies against a wall riddled with bullet holes at what looked like a place of summary execution. That's on the 17th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the references for that are P4397 and P4392. Actually, we can have a look at the article. P4397, please. If you could make it a little bigger?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Have a look at the article briefly and I'll have a question for you, Mr. Zametica.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very good. I have read it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Zametica, are these reports from Serb sources part of what you described in another press release on the 17th of July, part of what you described as an orgy of uncritical reporting aided by Muslim authorities?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this article actually confirms that. And I shall explain. First of all, to answer your initial question as to whether I had seen on the 17th of July this article in "The Independent," no, I did not see it. I have read it for the first time in my life right now, okay? So that's out of the way.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Zametica --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Zametica, if this is the first time that now you say you've read this article, we are going to move on. I don't want to spend any more time on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, he should be allowed to complete his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just let me read Ms. Edgerton's question. Yes, Mr. Zametica, please proceed to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Now, the article, which I have just seen for the first time in my life, in fact, confirms what I said in that statement on July the 17th about unverified and tendentious, I would say now, reporting by the Western media on the events in Srebrenica. You see, you -- you make a big deal out of the fact that this is from Serb sources. This is indeed a Serb source, which is -- is it B92? Which was a Studio B -- Studio B which was generally an anti-Bosnian Serb station. Its journalists -- its -- its policy was anti-Bosnian -- but it doesn't matter. Even Studio B despite its political bias against the Bosnian Serbs suggested that these Muslims -- these Muslim soldiers were killed in combat, "killed in combat." Now, this journalist called Robert Block, never heard of him before, although I followed these journalists, he then says, the scene -- I quote: "The scene, however, looked," repeat looked, "more like a place of summary execution than a combat." Now, he is giving his own personal impression about this particular horrible scene, but he himself is not sure whether these were indeed executions or these Muslim soldiers had been killed in the heat of battle. So he himself says "looked." What does it mean, "looked"? What evidence is there in this article to suggest that, you know, these people had been executed? He's simply saying, you know, putting forward his own subjective, probably bias, point of view and saying the place looked. Well, he can't use a stronger term because he's actually not sure and cannot prove it, but, you know, it's a good example of how you can twist words and how you can -- you can distort -- you can distort history.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But, Mr. Zametica, you can confirm now, can't you, that his speculation at the time --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- was correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in -- in this particular case, Your Honour, I'm not sure that it was or not. You know, I cannot say either yes or not because it looks as if this was -- it looks -- if they were prisoners executed -- I don't know. So, yes, I allow for the possibility that they were executed, but, I mean, from this particular article, one cannot be sure. That's all I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. As Dr. Karadzic's advisor, his spokesperson, his letter writer, a member of his immediate office, you would have been aware of formal letters from authorities in the international community that were directed to Dr. Karadzic; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: By and large, yes, if -- if he -- if he chose to show them to me. But he would have showed them -- if they were important, he would have showed them to me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. So Dr. Karadzic then would have showed you the formal letter that the Special Rapporteur of the Commission for Human Rights, Mr. Mazowiecki wrote on the 24th of July, protesting the forced displacement of 40.000 people from Srebrenica and noting that several thousand additional had been unaccounted for and asking for access to those who were detained. Because that's pretty important, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I hear you say -- sorry, this is not a question. I'm just trying to establish the date. Did I hear you say 24th of July?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. On 24th of July, I was in Montenegro, so he would not have shown me that letter because it would have been impossible for him to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So Dr. Karadzic would have shown you the letter from Mr. Akashi on 12 August 1995, expressing his concern that many of the former inhabitants of Srebrenica still weren't accounted for and noting the reports of mass graves that had been identified by the American government. And that same letter, actually, on the 12th of August, asks you to allow UNPROFOR to investigate the allegations. It requests access to UNPROFOR, members of UNHCR, ICRC, and other international agencies to the persons who had been displaced from Srebrenica and actually at that point from Zepa and were held in areas of -- under your control. He would have shown you that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. I must say I cannot remember. On the date that you mentioned, I think you said 12th of August, there were quite a few things going on. We just had an attempted coup d'état --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about a coup d'état, I asked you about a letter.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in that case --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I think that was said in the context why he couldn't remember that letter. Let him continue, Ms. Edgerton, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other important thing, apart from the coup d'état going on at the time, was the very serious military situation in the western parts of the country. So my answer to you is that Dr. Karadzic may have shown me this letter but I certainly cannot remember it. Although let me add this: If I actually saw it and read it, I may -- you know, I may remember it, I may remember that I read something similar a long time ago, but at the moment I cannot remember it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Zametica, you didn't conduct any investigation into the whereabouts of the people that Mr. Akashi noted were unaccounted for. You didn't conduct them at any time in July, you didn't conduct them at any time in August, and you didn't conduct them any time thereafter; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware - I repeat, I'm not aware - of that letter by Mr. Yasushi Akashi and I cannot add more to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My question is: You didn't conduct any investigation into the whereabouts of these people that Mr. Akashi happened to note were unaccounted for. That's the same group of people that Mr. Mazowiecki noted were unaccounted for. It's the same group of people that the international community was crying were unaccounted for. You didn't conduct any investigation at any time in July, any time in August, any time thereafter. You didn't conduct any investigation, did you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the context of what was happening at the time, in the western parts of Republika Srpska, I -- I really think that was probably something that I was most -- I personally was mostly preoccupied with but also Dr. Karadzic and -- and I don't know what Dr. Karadzic did in terms of responding to that letter that you say Mr. Akashi had written to him, so you better ask Mr. Karadzic about that, not me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I asked you whether or not at any time you conducted an investigation into the whereabouts of the people from Srebrenica who were unaccounted for. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Zametica, what you continued to say, in July of 1995, on the 31st of July actually, was that there was no ethnic cleansing, no atrocities, these are tales, these are lies. You said that, Mr. Zametica, to "USA Today" in reaction to the stories of survivors from Srebrenica who had made their way to Bosnian-held territory; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to see that article, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 65 ter number 25323.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The statement that I've just quoted to you is the fifth sentence from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in fact, this is a -- yet another confirmation of what I have been saying throughout, that at the time we were absolutely unaware of any atrocities having taken place, and this is what I said on the 17th of July, and this is what I also say on the 31st of July, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When did you come back from Montenegro, Mr. Zametica?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the end of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Fine. Mr. Zametica, this is untrue, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is untrue?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That there were no -- your statement that there was no ethnic cleansing, that there are no atrocities, that these are lies, is actually a lie itself?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm amazed that we are wasting so much time on this. I have already made my position, and I -- I've explained my position very clearly. At the time -- so let me repeat it. At the time I was unaware of any atrocities. Subsequently, I found out about the atrocities and I agree there was a massacre in Srebrenica. I said that yesterday, very clearly. And why are we going over and over this particular matter, when I have already stated, and admitted, there was a massacre in Srebrenica? I do not understand you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can I have that as a Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6477, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Zametica, these statements are cover-ups, just like that agreement is a cover-up of what actually happened in Srebrenica. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Zametica, I'm going to read you something that you said in 1997 during the course of an interview with journalist Jovan Janjic and it appeared in "Nin" in an article entitled: "Karadzic won't go to The Hague." You said: "The raison d'être of the Tribunal is precisely to convict Karadzic and Mladic. That is the Serbian nation. People should understand that the establishment of this ad hoc Tribunal in The Hague is an unprecedented legal farce in the history of the United Nations." Do you still stand by that, Mr. Zametica?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I please have the article? I would like to see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Zametica, this is a "yes" or "no" question. Do you stand by the proposition I've just put to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to see the original in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't have any difficulty with showing the document to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, nor do I, Your Honours. 65 ter number 25243.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But the Serbian version, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I would need a minute to -- if we go over to the next page, please, in Serbian. And by the way, the English reference is pages 6 and 7. Oh, I've got that wrong as well. I think I was working on different English version. For the English if we could go back to the previous, preceding page. Apologies. What I'm going to do is look at my hard copy and identify the proper passage in -- or the proper page number in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think it's at the top of page 4, maybe the end of page 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not trying to be difficult but I really cannot see the small -- the small print in the Serbian version. I'm very keen to actually see the exact part, if you can -- if you have ways and means to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can collapse English part for some time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we can collapse the English, yes. Yes, I have read it. The translation isn't exact but it's -- I mean, I don't have major objections. So to answer your questions, no, I no longer stand by that. I have changed my mind with regard to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And how have you changed your mind, Mr. Zametica?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I shall answer your question. Recently, this Tribunal acquitted -- acquitted the former head of Serbian state security, Mr. Stanisic, and in the light of that acquittal, I thought about again this Tribunal and I now realise that this Tribunal is a fair one.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just your indulgence for a moment. I'd like to check something. Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, and pardon me, could we have this document, 65 ter number 25243, tendered as a Prosecution exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6478, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it you have some questions for your re-examination. Shall we have a break or would you like to go on?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can take a break, Your Excellency, if that is what you believe is good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I will leave it to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then let us take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We shall have a break for half an hour and resume at 10 to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Dr. Zametica. You were asked earlier today if you had carried out any investigations into the allegations that some people were unaccounted for, and you were asked about exchanges of prisoners. I should like to ask you: In your experience, was it the first time that we had any prisoners? In other words, in three and a half years of war, had we ever faced circumstances in which prisoners of war were liquidated?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certainly aware that, in the course of the war, we had prisoners, just like the other side or sides had our prisoners, and it was common practice to exchange those prisoners. I'm certainly not aware that we had ever, as you put it, liquidated any of those prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were shown the diary of the late Professor Koljevic, who wrote, among other things, about the capture of UN personnel during air strikes, and also about Srebrenica. So I'd like to show you an excerpt.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we pull up in e-court, 1D09847, please? Page 1. We can remove the cover page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please focus on paragraph 3. I'll read: [In English] "In the meantime, between the second and third strikes, Tuzla was shelled and a scene occurred from which it would be very difficult to establish what had happened. Most probably a massacre of civilians had been staged near a restaurant in Tuzla, similar to those which happened in Vase Miskina Street and at the Markale Market. It is very unlikely that any of our people would have done something like that on their own initiative, and certainly no one received such an order because it would be just insane at this moment." [Interpretation] How does this fit in with your experience of these setups and propaganda?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that in my statement, there is a mention of one such incident, that's the Markale incident in, I think, February 1994. And I think I say in my statement that it looked as if this was a staged massacre. However, to this day, I really do not know the truth of the matter. I think I said that, you know, this has not been conclusively established. But one suspects that something like that would have played to the interest of the Muslim side, for obvious propaganda reasons, and it was fully used by them for propaganda purposes. It brought them the sympathies of the world. From that point of view, I would not be surprised if the incident in Tuzla to which you have just drawn my attention and which is being talked about in Professor Koljevic's diary, I would not be surprised if that too were in that category. However, I must emphasise I have no knowledge, and I cannot say anything with any certainty regarding this matter. I should add that it would certainly have -- as Professor Koljevic said, it would certainly be against the Serb interests to do anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this page be admitted into evidence, from Professor Koljevic's diary, although it would be good to admit both books in their entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zametica said he had no knowledge about this and then all the important answers were recorded. Do we have to admit it still? Mr. Robinson, could you assist us?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I think since we covered this ground with Deronjic and you decided to admit it -- but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But in this case, that important part was read out and it's in the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. No, I think in this case it's sufficient that what's been read out can be enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Just for purposes of clarification, I was more interested in whether Dr. Zametica was aware of this pattern, and what our knowledge was on the whole, and to what extent we could have any trust. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Zametica, you were asked quite a bit about our knowledge as to what happened in Srebrenica. So I'd like to show you another excerpt from 1D9748, Professor Koljevic's diary. While we are waiting for that, did we have several civilian commissioners for Srebrenica or only one, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember how many commissars, civilian commissars, for Srebrenica we had.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have page 3 now? And if we could -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please focus on the last paragraph: [In English] "Most immensely -- mostly immense media pressure is being exerted on us again. There is talk of the greatest ethnic cleansing even though the Muslims left Srebrenica voluntarily, in the presence of UNPROFOR. I discussed this with our newly appointed commissioner in Srebrenica, who was a student at the faculty of philosophy in Sarajevo some ten years ago, and from him I heard that there really had been no killing of civilians and how the Muslims did not want to remain in Srebrenica either out of fear because they were aware of what their combatants had done to the Serbs in the surrounding area due to the threat of Sarajevo -- threats from Sarajevo. They were ordered to leave directly from Sarajevo." [Interpretation] How does this fit in? This is the 21st of July, 1995, his encounter with our civilian commissioner. How does this fit into what you know and what your experience was?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you remember, I was already away from Pale in Montenegro on that particular day, so I would not have talked to Professor Koljevic about it, even though I would meet him on a regular basis, on a daily basis, almost as frequently as I would meet you. But, yes, I mean, I can well believe that what Professor Koljevic wrote here is entirely correct. I should add as a general point that Professor Koljevic's diary is, in my subjective view, a very important source on the events of -- on the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina during the war. He used to -- it's a very authentic source. He used to dictate into a dictaphone the events of the day, late at night before he went to bed, and the following day, I think his secretary would type this. So they constitute a very, very authentic source for everything that was going on. And to this I should add that Professor Koljevic was a man of great personal integrity and he would not be making things up in his diary. So that's the general point I wanted to make in that connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Zametica. Is there any relevance in the fact that already in mid-January 1997, Dr. Koljevic was no longer with us? And after that, he was no longer in a position to make any entries in his diary?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't quite understood your question. Can you please rephrase it or repeat it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably you overlapped with the translation. Please repeat your answer. And in the future, please put a pause before answering the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask you when, to the best of your knowledge, Professor Koljevic passed away.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is well known. He committed suicide in, I think, January 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have a close relationship with Professor Koljevic, or, rather, were you in close contact with him when you were in Dayton during the negotiations there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We didn't talk about this, about Professor Koljevic during the cross-examination. This is far and away outside the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Koljevic's diary was discussed in the direct examination, not in the cross?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, a page, an entry from his diary was discussed. We did not discuss any further than the diary. We did not discuss the witness's relationship with Koljevic, Koljevic's presence at Dayton, what's being put to the witness now, and that, I think, is outside of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now I see the point. Would you like to add anything, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think if Dr. Karadzic would just show the witness the next document the relevance will be apparent.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just respond briefly. Dr. Zametica characterised this document as a first-rate document and that is why I wanted to establish until when this diary could have been kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So now the question is whether you were on the delegation together while you were in Dayton and were you in contact?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Professor Koljevic was a member of the Republika Srpska delegation at the Dayton peace talks, as indeed I was, and we were in daily contact. So, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D09751 in e-court? Page 3, please. This is the entry for the 19th of November, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at the first paragraph of that entry. Or if necessary, I can read it out. [In English] "But The Hague anti-Serbian campaign continued mercilessly to the end. On Friday, 17th of November, the New York Times again poured forth its verbal artillery against Karadzic and Mladic with fresh and horrific alleged details from Srebrenica of how Muslim children had been killed in front of their mothers, and a grandfather had been made to eat his grandson's liver. If these were true, those Serbian soldiers should not be sent to The Hague but to a Serbian summary court for the most drastic punishment for besmirching the name of the Serbs. Fortunately, however, but also sadly, these stories resemble too closely the previous imaginative 'testimony' of our former neighbours, and it is absolutely impossible to believe any such things." [Interpretation] How does this relate to your experience regarding what appeared in the media against us? To what extent could it be believed? And to what extent did you share this experience with Professor Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, what Professor Koljevic wrote about in his diary, which pertains to the period he was at Dayton, so he was obviously reading US press there, that's something we were aware of. But at the time, I must say we were far more worried, not about the propaganda being carried out against the Bosnian Serbs, rather we were concerned about the course of the conference, so it wasn't a huge subject between us. I should add one point because this is taking place during the Dayton conference, I must say that during the Dayton conference, although we had as a delegation, and as individuals within that delegation of Republika Srpska, frequent contacts with representatives of international organisations present there, and practically everyone was present, the European Union was present, the Contact Group was present --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Zametica. I'm wondering where we are heading now at the moment. I'm not sure whether it arises out of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked Dr. Zametica whether he shared this experience with Professor Koljevic, and Dr. Zametica wanted to say what it was that they got in Dayton. That is the end of November. In relation to the information that we had. It's a question of the extent of our information, the degree to which we were informed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think Dr. Zametica answered your question. And if you have more, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: During the conference in Dayton, did you receive some more information orally, verbally, in addition to what the media said? At the conference was the crime in Srebrenica one of the topics?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was about to begin answering that, in fact, when His Honour intervened, so let me continue. Although everyone was present at Dayton from the international community, as I began enumerating the European Union, the Contact Group and so on, the United Nations, of course, and the conference took place over three weeks, it lasted three weeks, so a long time, no one, but no one, from the international community ever, to my knowledge, raised the subject of Srebrenica with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the last question is of semantic nature, rather. When you said that I was a weak president, did you mean that I was a bad president? As the media maliciously --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I don't think Ms. Edgerton touched upon that issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Correct. I did not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But there is this problem of phraseology. The English phrase is being translated in a different way into our language so I just wanted it to be put -- well, just half a sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I can reformulate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While the issue does not arise from the line of cross-examination, it seems to be related to the translation or meaning of some words so we will -- on that basis we will allow you to continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Zametica, during the cross-examination as well, what was being challenged was your position that I did not exercise control, probably relying on what you said in constitutional terms, in terms of the constitutional concept of the Presidency. You said that I was a weak president. Tell us what you meant by that. Was I a bad president or was I a president who did not control the institutions that also operated?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you have raised a legitimate point regarding this translation question. The English term "weak" translates into the Serbian language as "slab," s-l-a-b. Now, that in the Serbian language has a double meaning. It can mean weak in the English sense, or it can mean bad in the sense of not a good one. Therefore, I wish to emphasise here, when I said you were a weak president, I did not mean to say you were a bad president. I meant weak in the English sense of weak.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I've just looked at the transcript for the last two days, the word "weak" was never mentioned so I don't know where this arises, but it could be my misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was during his direct examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But during the cross, it was challenged, Dr. Zametica's position with regard to the control I had and the insight I had, control over processes and institutions. An attempt was made to prove through intercepts that there was rapid communication --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's leave it there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Zametica. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, that concludes your evidence, Mr. Zametica. On behalf of the Chamber, and the Tribunal as a whole, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it the next witness is ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. It's General Milenko Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Excellencies, should we tender those pages or you think it was read in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's sufficient to have what was read out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sir, if you could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, General Zivanovic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you commence your evidence, General, I must draw your attention to a certain rule that we have here at the Tribunal. That is Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled in such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understood that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, General Zivanovic. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please could we both abide by this minor technical detail? Could we pause between my questions and your answers in order to save time because otherwise we would have to repeat things and have things corrected because time is required to interpret my sentences and yours.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will do my best that we are both properly heard and that we are all understood in good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You were still too quick to start answering the question before the translation is finished. Please put a sufficient pause. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, did you give a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have in e-court 1D09060.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your statement, you will see now. You can identify it and tell us whether that's it. What you see on the screen, is that your statement?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the last page please be shown to the witness so that he can identify the signature there?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, have you read and signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the statement faithfully reflect what you communicated to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does reflect it correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just a bit of patience, please. I'm afraid that this is the previous version that has been downloaded. It should have been a more recent one. Between the first statement and the proofing you had here, did you make any corrections?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, one particular item, and I also added a few new points, and that was signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So that is after the 9th of June, so it was done now in November -- no, rather, October?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will have that version too. Could you please tell us the following: If I were to put the same questions to you today in the courtroom, would your answers be the same as those provided in the final version of this statement?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Has the addendum been uploaded on a separate number?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It's 1D9753. If we could call that, I think that would correct it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I wanted to see the previous one but both were in e-court. Could we please show the last page now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The 27th of October, is that the day when you signed the reviewed statement?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's it, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I tender this 92 ter statement to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
