utterances.text: We shall deal with the associated exhibits separately. Do you have any objection to the statement and the addendum, Ms. Pack? Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: None, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one question. It's about paragraph 40 and 41, where he says he did not take part in the alleged intercepted conversation. What's the relevance? I had difficulty understanding why this is being tendered. Are you going to pre-empt the Prosecution in case it is minded to tender this intercept?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think that was the idea, but we don't have to pursue that. If you don't want to admit those, then it's not necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me ask, Ms. Pack, whether you're minded to deal with these two intercepts, otherwise we will order them -- the Defence to delete those two paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I didn't intend to deal with 40 and those two particular intercepts, no. In fact, I could perhaps assist with one of them. It's been admitted in any event, coming from a different source, as P05294. That's a redacted version, under seal as P05293 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which one is that?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: That's the one that's identified as 1D09010.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then it's important to leave the paragraph there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Well, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Whether -- because he's still dealing -- I'm not --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: That's a matter for the -- that's a matter for the accused, but so far as the Prosecution is concerned, I'm just clarifying that so it's clear to the Chamber that that intercept is an intercept that has separately, from another source, been admitted. And the following paragraph is similarly referencing the contents, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Separate from the admissibility or admission, then we'll -- the statement as well as the addendum as they are. Shall we give -- assign the numbers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does the addendum contain the previous statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Thank you. We will admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The 65 ter number 1D9753 will be Exhibit D3932.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Aside from those two intercepts, do you have any objection to the associated exhibits, Ms. Pack?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, I do have some observations in relation to those. So far as 1D09017, it's a small observation, but there is no foundation laid for the admission of the photos at pages 1 and 3 of this -- the document as uploaded, only the one at page 2. So far as 1D09025 is concerned, that is apparently an article -- an interview of -- it is an interview of the witness but it's at pages 1 and 2 only of the document uploaded, so I would oppose the admission of the third page which is a second article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You said the last two digits is 25?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it not a letter? The 65 ter number, the interview, seems to be ending with 27.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. I'm very grateful to you, Mr. President. Yes, that's absolutely right. So that is the document to which I was referring. And it's the first two pages, which is where the interview is located. So far as another two documents are concerned, P04553, which is a presidential order of the 14th of July, there is no foundation laid in paragraph 36 for the admission of that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does it not mean that it has been already admitted?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It has but there is -- it's already been admitted but it just -- it may well be that the wrong exhibit is referenced in the statement and indeed it is sought to admit the wrong exhibit. But I'm -- I refer the Chamber to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think the Defence is tendering that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Okay. And so far as one further exhibit is concerned, P05291, I would just caution that that has previously been admitted under seal. So, so far it is referenced by -- in the court, that that should remain the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. So as to those intercepts, one is already admitted, as indicated by Ms. Pack, so there is no problem with it. But with the remainder, 1D9018, there is no basis to admit it. So shall we -- we will not admit it. And then as the Chamber finds that following documents does not form an inseparable or indispensable part of the statement or that -- or the witness did not sufficiently discuss those documents, and they are: 1D9003, discussed in para 17; 1D9016, discussed in para 47; and -- and that's it. So we will not admit those documents. And finally, 1D9021 is his separate statement, so to speak. So I'm not sure whether this kind of document can be admitted as an associated exhibit. So if the Defence is minded to tender this document, I would instruct the accused to lead it live. So I think I made the ruling sufficiently clear. And finally, I take it that Defence has no difficulty to admit only page 2 as indicated by Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. And also with respect to 9027, we will just admit pages 1 and 2 of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I missed that. The Chamber doesn't think that that also -- that does not form inseparable and indispensable part of the statement. So we will not admit it either. So if the Defence finds it important, it should lead live. So with that caveat, the remaining documents will be admitted into evidence and assigned numbers in due course by the Registrar. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now read the short summary of General Milenko Zivanovic's statement in the English language, and it's the statement that has just been admitted. [In English] General Milenko Zivanovic served as commander of the Drina Corps of the Bosnian Serb Army, VRS, in November -- from November 1992 until July 1995. The main task of the Drina Corps was to defend the Serbian people in the Podrinje area of Eastern Bosnia. The Muslim forces in the enclaves of Srebrenica, Zepa and Gorazde were constantly launching attacks against Serbian civilians. They torched the Serbian homes and killed women, children and the elderly. The Drina Corps advocated a genuine demilitarisation of the area but that never happened. Despite the lack of demilitarisation of the enclaves, General Zivanovic facilitated the delivery of humanitarian aid to the population in those areas by the United Nations and international humanitarian organisations. After the Bosnian Muslims had expanded the boundaries of the Srebrenica enclave so as to connect it to Zepa and use that connection to smuggle weapons into the Srebrenica enclave in July 1995, the Drina Corps commenced an effort to separate the enclaves. After that effort had commenced, General Zivanovic had a telephone conversation with President Karadzic which was recorded. During that conversation, President Karadzic insisted that UN personnel stationed in Srebrenica be treated correctly. There was never any plan to displace or kill Bosnian Muslims of Srebrenica and he never spoke with President Karadzic about any such plan. General Zivanovic had another telephone conversation with President Karadzic the night after the Bosnian Serb Army had entered Srebrenica. President Karadzic inquired about the number of casualties and appeared satisfied when told that there had been no casualties. There was never any discussion between General Zivanovic and President Karadzic about the execution of prisoners. From his knowledge of President Karadzic, General Zivanovic is confident that President Karadzic would never be in favour of or condone the execution of prisoners. General Zivanovic had no knowledge of any plan to execute prisoners from Srebrenica and had no idea anyone would do such a thing. General Zivanovic never informed President Karadzic that prisoners from Srebrenica would be, were being, or had been executed. General Zivanovic never saw any written report or document in which the execution of prisoners from Srebrenica was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before I allow you to be cross-examined by the Prosecution, I would ask you, General, whether you brought with you and handed over to the Defence one map?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show in e-court 1D9755? Could we please zoom in?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And can you please read aloud the title of this map? What does it map represent and why is it important?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This map is a document which was in my office from the moment when it was drawn up, that is to say, February 1993, up until -- let me say, well, it has survived to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And why is it important? What does it show? Why is it important?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The title on the map reads: "Overview of the destruction of Serbian villages in the area of Srebrenica and Bratunac municipalities from May 1992 until January 1993." So no enclaves are mentioned here as yet. This is the beginning of the war conflict in the said areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And who produced this map?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The map was made by my professional organs under my personal supervision. Why? Because it's a document that is crucially truthful, which showed and demonstrated that the Serbian people in these areas has practically been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell the Chamber what happened after January 1993 and why? In the conflict in this -- first of all, why was it only in January or, rather, February 1993 that you stopped such a situation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you look at the map as a whole, it shows that, in fact, more than 90 per cent of the territory of the areas of the Srebrenica and Bratunac municipalities were physically destroyed. It is clearly depicted on the map where the Muslim armed forces from Srebrenica attacked by month. Please, if we could show the key of the map, because there are different symbols here. You can stop now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When was the Drina Corps established and why?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Drina Corps was established on the 1st of November, 1992, with the main purpose not to allow the Serbian people in the area between Zvornik and Visegrad to be completely wiped out, including the Romanija municipalities of Han Pijesak, Sokolac, and Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you now explain these colours a little bit for us? Please, what do these forms and shapes mean, the rectangles and the circles?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: These symbols, the topographic symbols on the map, as we, the soldiers, would call them, show by month the axis of the movement of the enemy forces, that is to say, the Muslim forces, through the Serbian populated areas. And the circles that we can see here are the results of the activities of Muslim forces in May 1992, as the key says. Each of these circles stands at a place of one independent Serbian settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please, please. Which means, which means, if you allow me, which means that where a circle has been placed, that village was destroyed. Whoever could be killed was killed or wounded or went missing, and those who were lucky managed to run away. Looking at the results of what happened in the month of May, if we look at the key, we can then see what were the attacks launched in June. For June we used the squares, as you can see. We are now showing with a pointer at the village where I was born. The 21st of June was the date. The village was completely razed with the surrounding hamlets and with all its inhabitants, destroyed, destroyed. And if we could please stop here for a moment, with a further explanation of the -- of the map itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pack?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, if this is going to continue into a protracted examination of alleged crimes again Serbian civilians, then I'm afraid I have to object. This is evidence that -- the Trial Chamber has already said that any evidence -- it won't accept tu quoque evidence as it has no impact on the accused's responsibility for the crimes charged, so my objection is on that basis. And I think I've allowed a few questions in, but so far as they continue, I oppose them and I would oppose admission of this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, what I wish to elicit from this witness were the reasons for establishing an existence of the Drina Corps, both the reasons and the purpose, and the plans of the Muslim armed forces which conditioned the conduct of the Drina Corps. It's not tu quoque. I'm not looking for any sort of justification but an understanding why was the Drina Corps set up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber allowed you to continue because it may be related to understand the background and the reason for the establishment of Drina Corps, whether it's relevant or not. But it does not help anybody if you go into too much -- too much detail.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, as obviously we do not have enough time, could I please ask you to summarise for the Chamber the villages -- the circles stand for the villages that were torched in May, the squares in June, and how about the oval shapes and so on? And can you tell us what were the goals of the BH Army which resulted in the forming of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As I said, we can see in the key these various geometrical forms which are placed on the locations where certain settlements were destroyed by months and ending with the 17th of January, 1993. And the number 157 individual settlements which had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What were the goals? What was the purpose for which these armed forces were doing that in our rear? First of all, where was the front line facing the main part of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, these villages were unprotected. There were no front lines there as such, because up to number 42, up until the 19th of May, 1992, the JNA was responsible for this area, the Yugoslav People's Army. So they ought to be asked what were their reports about the destruction of these villages and the end of any life in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any particular reasons for which the BH Army wanted to keep this zone in war, and fighting?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: One doesn't need to be very wise to understand that this is the classical ethnic cleansing of an area, from the non-Muslim population. I'm not sure how else I could express it. In other words, not a single house was skipped, not a single Serbian family was left to live in its own area. And if that were to be allowed, then there would have been no end to the massacres. So that was the main message, that a corps, an operative force, would have to be formed which would cover all these areas and prevent complete destruction of the Serbian population in the said areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please explain for us the military reasons, the strategic reasons, for preventing these activities in terms of communication and so on?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's understandable that every communication, peacetime communication, in these areas would stop, especially as communication along the Drina River was cut off. And there is proof that they planned to destroy the Bajina Basta hydroelectric power plant which would have caused a tsunami such as has never been seen there. Then the area is important for the ores with which it is rich. Everything was cut off, the life stopped. It was frozen. Natural life was practically dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was the composition of the Drina Corps in military terms? Where did its people come from? Were they professional soldiers, and can you tell us who did you command over?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The military composition of the Drina Corps, it was made up of able-bodied Serbian population from these areas, including, as I said, the municipalities of Zvornik and Visegrad. Let me say Sokolac as well, Rogatica, and all the areas from there towards the Drina. There were some of us professional officers, professional JNA officers, who were natives from this area and our task was to set up the corps, to order the units, and to prevent further exodus of the people in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that those who were lucky, from the destroyed villages, had managed to flee and that they were fortunate. Did you have any soldiers who hailed from the destroyed villages?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The majority of the soldiers of the Drina Corps hailed precisely from the areas where the villages had been destroyed. So overnight they had become homeless, so to speak, because when I checked the lists of the unit members, and their personal documents, the majority of the people in the corps were from these areas. Those were the areas. That was how the subordinate commands got their names, the Milici, Han Pijesak, Sekovici and other units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have any problems with keeping them under control? What was the state of mind of these people who had lost everything, their villages and their property, their relatives? Did you have to deal with that? What was the state of mind of these people?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: To be sincere, the command made considerable efforts not to return evil with evil, not to pay back, but when the conditions were created to re-establish life but to prevent any instances of revenge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this map be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Pack?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not been translated so I would ask that before it's admitted it's translated. I won't oppose its admission otherwise, having in mind what Your Honour has indicated. That's my only objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, 65 ter number 1D9755 will be MFI D3954.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. At this moment, I have no further questions for General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General Zivanovic, as you have noted, your evidence-in-chief in this case has been admitted in writing in most part in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, Ms. Pack. Please proceed, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: General, you spoke to the accused's investigator, Milomir Savcic, on the 20th of March, 2013; is that right? Do you remember talking to him and telling him --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You told him you had received death threats. You said there was a group of Muslim extremists in Vienna that had put a price on your head, and that whoever brought your head on a platter would receive gold, that you wouldn't testify whatever the cost. Do you remember saying those things?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Now, Milomir Savcic didn't believe you. He said he thought that the reasons given by you were not true and were unjustified, and that, in fact, you had been instructed not to testify. Is that right? You weren't telling the truth to the accused's investigator?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please, you have to understand that I'm telling only the truth, and I've lived only with the truth all my life. What you just said, the last part, that I was instructed not to testify, who said that? Where was it said?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm just going to refer to 65 ter 25455, please, which is the official note from Milomir Savcic of his conversation with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Now, this is in English so I'm going to have to read out the last paragraph for you. "I believe that the reasons given by Mr. Zivanovic are not true and are therefore unjustified. I believe that he has been instructed to refuse to testify," and it continues. Did you fabricate death threats to avoid having to testify?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. None of this stands. I don't know how the gentleman Mr. Savcic, came to this conclusion because I know the man from the war. He did not introduce himself to me officially. Instead he came to me, accompanied by a journalist, to meet like former comrades-in-arms and we talked, formally and informally, about our adventures from before the war and during the war. And as to this allegation that I lied and I don't want to testify, that's not true. I am a war veteran, disabled. My lungs are punctured. I suffer from high blood pressure and diabetes, but precisely for the sake of truth and my whole life with all its trials and tribulations, I wanted to come here, and I'm really honoured to be here, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not recorded that the general said he still has shrapnel inside his body.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I said bullets. If you allow me --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: We'll move on, please. Now the Drina Corps was formed on the 1st of November, 1992, and you were appointed its commander, right? On the 8th of --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: On the 8th of November, soon after the formation of the corps, you attended a meeting with the accused, with General Mladic, with the Defence Minister, Subotic, Krajisnik, other corps commanders. You remember that, that meeting on the 8th, took all day?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please, you have to understand, there were several meetings. As for the precise day, after 20 years, the substance of the meeting and all the details, I would have to analyse this in depth to be able to recall everything. Yes, I did attend several such meetings, but I have to tell you none of them, at least to the best of my recollection, was not about any wrongdoing, misdeeds. None of these meetings led into any violation of the rules and customs of war. That is my answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can we have P01481, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm going to help with you remembering that meeting. This is an extract from the handwritten notebook of Mladic. I'm going to take you to the entry dated 8th November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It's in the English e-court at page 141, and in the B/C/S at page 141. Actually, can we have the B/C/S transcript as opposed to the handwritten original? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: These are Mladic's notes of the meeting that you attended on the 8th of November, 1992. And you can see it's a meeting with the corps commanders; right? Look at the heading at the top, the date at the top, and the time.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: That helps you remember you attended that meeting. It was with Karadzic and others. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I never said I didn't attend. Of course, I did, and every document you show me is of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can we look at page 143? In both B/C/S and English.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You can see at point 5 there you're mentioned. And there you say the corps is living through its eighth day. So you remember being there, saying something similar?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: We can go, please, to page 146 -- 145, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: There we have, halfway down the page, President Karadzic, notes of what he is saying in that meeting. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I see this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: We can turn to the following page, please, 146.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And we can see President Karadzic there concluding at the bottom of the entry which is noting what he has said, says: Maybe it would be good if we solved the issue of the Drina. If you look at the left screen, that's got the B/C/S in it, I think. Have you got it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And after Karadzic speaks, we have Krajisnik. Yes? You can see that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And he begins, "I admire the military successes," and you can read along in the B/C/S while I'm reading out the English. "Which is very dangerous to seize their territories, the Drina and the Neretva, we have a disproportionate engagement of the army in relation to the strategic objectives."

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: That's over the page, so we can go to page 147, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: He continued: "We have not achieved the Neretva, the sea and the Podrinje area. We have achieved the corridor, separation with the Muslims." And then he goes on: "We must bring the war to an end. The most pressing thing is to mop up Orasje and then to solve the problem of the Podrinje area and the Neretva valley area" -- sorry, "the Neretva River valley as soon as possible. The Muslims must not stay with us and they should not be given any kind of autonomy. The most important objective is the task assigned to Zivanovic, the mopping up of the Drina. The most important task is separation from the Muslims."

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There is nothing bad about this. When you see the reference to the mopping up of the Drina, what is meant are all these villages that we saw on the map a moment ago, devastated Serb areas. And if only I were able to show you the maps of Sekovic, Zvornik, Han Pijesak, then his statement would be more easily understandable. But further below it says "separation from the Muslims," it doesn't say "kill the Muslims." It says "separation from them." If anybody had, God forbid, told me --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: That's right. Wait a second. Wait.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sorry, we'll take it easy.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Let's take it in stages, please.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You agree that he says what is recorded here. You agree that that is what he said at this meeting. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, he did say that. That's not in dispute. I don't know what we are talking about here, whether I agreed with -- with whoever said whatever at the meeting. But this thing about the enemy, this is their free speech. It doesn't say kill the Muslims anywhere. It says separation. If anybody had mentioned the killing of Muslims to me, they would have never seen me again.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: But if they say ethnic cleansing, that's okay?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, could we be shown where mopping up is shown to mean ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What ethnic cleansing? Do you see the map we just looked at? It's like leopard skin, throughout. There were 157 villages where everybody was killed. A Serb could not enter those villages to pluck a plum off the tree. Whoever went in was as good as dead. That's the problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You knew, didn't you, General, that yours was the most important task remaining for the VRS, and that task, General, that task was the ethnic cleansing of the Podrinje; right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Overruled. Overruled. Please continue, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You yourself believed, didn't you, that there was no room for co-existence with the Muslims in the Podrinje; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If you only knew how much life I spent living together with the Muslims before the war and during the war, you would never ask me this question. I offered my blood for the Muslim wounded. I rescued Muslims. The Muslims invited me to serve as their commander. They wanted me as their commander. Do you imagine how much effort we made to help these people? You are trying to paint me here as a henchman. You should not be doing this. You should ask my Muslim friends, close friends, some of whom are my best men at my wedding, what they think.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You, the commander of the Drina Corps, you would never have said something like: There is no room for co-existence? That's not the sort of thing you would say?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, wait a minute. Wait a minute. What kind of co-existence can you have if you have a front line between two warring parties? But when the war is over, when the front line exists no more, we have no choice but to live together. That is the alpha and omega in our region. We have to live together, whereas individual perpetrators should be held to account, brought to justice. The lofty aim of all of us, including this honourable Tribunal, is to create a better quality of life in our region.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'd like to look at 1D09027, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I just want to refer you very quickly to an extract of an interview that you gave to interview [sic] on the 22nd of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to page 3, please in the English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's my house. Where did you get this? This is my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Now, let me just ask you to look, please, at one part of this which is the second column, please. Second column on the second page of the B/C/S, there we go. Thank you. And it's the second paragraph down in that second column and I'm just going to read it out to you. And you can perhaps indicate that you have the right section. You say -- you claim: "While our army is respecting the agreement in a disciplined manner," this is referring to the enclaves which had been established, "they are evading it in the" --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can follow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Let me read it out in English and you can follow the B/C/S: [As read] "... they are evading it in the belief that the status of the safety zones they will give them more time. But as commander of a corps that has resolved the military part of the problem in Podrinje, my message to them is: Don't fool yourselves. They should not succumb to collective hysteria but accept the outcome they have tailored for themselves, and once again we offer them an honourable epilogue. In this, I have to be sincere. There is no room for co-existence. It only mean that my Ratkovici and Ducici," which are your villages you referred to, "will never again fear death at the hands of a stranger, a knife in the back." Then you say: "I know the norm of the international community is that everyone should return to his hearth. But I say that there are no more hearths, only ashes." And then you continue. Now --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The burned-down hearths of our houses. Look at the date, look at the date that you've shown me yourself when this journalist wrote this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You -- you, General, you --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could I ask you, do you know that I, without Karadzic knowing, without Mladic knowing, although I know that Karadzic would have approved it 100 per cent, and that's why I did it, I established a hotline between my forces and the Muslim forces. That was February 1993. And I suggested more than once that everybody should stay in their homes that were not devastated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you continue, General Zivanovic, I would like you to answer the question first. Ms. Pack asked you whether you said this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a formulation authored by the journalist. You see the photograph showing my burned-down house, the doorstep of my house, and on another photograph you see the devastated cemetery where my parents were buried. In those circumstances, could we talk about co-existence? Yes, co-existence is possible, but only when those who had been responsible for crimes are brought to justice.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The translation is not good. This photograph is the -- shows the house where he was born, and in the English translation, we didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was a very, very hard day in my life, when I came and saw the debris, all that remained of my house, and the cemetery where my parents were buried, destroyed. Who could have had anything against my parents? My mother had fed more Muslim children than her own.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Let's keep to this document, please. You don't deny, then, saying those words; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At this time, with those feelings, I could have said even harsher words but I didn't. I did not sign this, by the way. This is an article authored by the journalist that reflects certain thoughts. But to talk about co-existence on that day, when I came to my birthplace and saw what I saw, I have to ask you and myself and everyone: Who defended my village, whose army? Whose army was it that defended my village?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry, but I don't think you're still answering the question. Could you answer the question? Shall I ask Ms. Pack to ask the question again?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just caution that the transcript is not entirely correct. Maybe that creates a false impression. General Zivanovic says, "I do not renounce the thoughts expressed in this interview, but this was authored by the journalist." The fact that General Zivanovic said, "I do not renounce the thoughts expressed in the interview" is missing from the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I leave it to you, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, again, again it was not recorded that the witness said, "And that is the answer."

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You don't renounce what was your view and your task, which was to -- to live in a Podrinje that was free of Muslims; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. Please don't -- that we separate, that we should separate.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd just like to admit that one page of that document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I would ask that this document be admitted in its entirety. It was an associated exhibit. It shows, for example, the photograph of his house that he refers to in his statement. He didn't seem to indicate exactly why it wouldn't be part of his -- a comprehensive part of his statement, but in any event, now that it's been used and he's explained the photographs as well as the text, I think it should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I don't oppose admission of the whole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me take a brief look at paragraph 16. Just a second. Very well. We will admit it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As a Prosecution exhibit or Defence Exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we would appreciate it if it could be admitted as a Defence Exhibit, although it's not a big point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Pack?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Don't oppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We shall admit it as a Defence Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3955, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we take a break, Ms. Pack? If it is convenient.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will have a break for 45 minutes and resume at quarter past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Directive 4, we're going to talk about directive 4. It was the first directive to regulate the activities of the Drina Corps, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: P00976, please. I just ask, please, for the English page 5 and in the B/C/S page 11.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm just going to ask you to deal with one paragraph which I've no doubt you know well. It's under the heading: "Tasks of the units," and this is the tasks for the Drina Corps, D. And you can see it's the second paragraph there in the B/C/S -- I'm sorry, is it page 11 you have there of the B/C/S? Yes. You can see what it says. I'm just going to read it out: From its present positions its main forces are to defend with the utmost persistence, Visegrad, Zvornik and the corridor, while the rest of its forces in the wider Podrinje region are to exhaust the enemy, inflict the heaviest possible losses on them, and force them to leave the Birac, Zepa and Gorazde areas with the Muslim population. Right? Very familiar with this order, this directive?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: We are going to go to P02085 which is your document, your Drina Corps command document, which followed directive 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can we have, please, first page in both languages?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And we see of course, and you agree, this order derived from directive 4, it was issued pursuant to directive 4; that's right, isn't it? Yes?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And I'd like you to look, please, at the first paragraph, the paragraph 1. You ordered this: Launch an attack against the main body of troops and major equipment to inflict on the enemy the highest possible losses, exhaust them, break them or force them to surrender, and force the Muslim local population to abandon the area of Cerska, Zepa, Srebrenica, and Gorazde. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And this is what you understood to be the task assigned to you under directive 4, right, to force -- included forcing the Muslim population to abandon the area, forcing the Muslim population out; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But that Muslim population was staying at Serb villages and had taken Serb property too. Why? Because whenever they took a territory, they would not allow Serb citizens any kind of access. I'm not talking about Serb soldiers. I'm talking about proprietors, civilians. When people who were Serbs tried to enter their own village, they would be killed. So that is the factual situation. That population that was in our areas was supposed to leave those areas, to my mind it is understandable to this day. If my brother returns to his own village to his own home, to the burned remains of his home, he has this Muslim waiting there for him, in his house, on his field. I'm not going to send my brother to a Muslim village, I'm going to send him to his own village. That would be the essence of my response to this paragraph number 1. You have to understand this. I repeat: No Serbs were allowed access to a single square metre of territory that they had taken, ever.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You'll have to help me understand your evidence, General. You are saying, are you, that the areas identified in your order, the areas Cerska, Zepa, Srebrenica and Gorazde, what are you saying, these are Serbian areas, these are burned Serbian homes, where you planned to -- you planned to replace the Muslim population with Serbs? I don't understand what your point is.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "Srebrenica," look at the hydroelectric power plant at Bajina Basta and then go up to Drinjaca, that was Srebrenica to my mind. When I say "Cerska," I'm referring to all the villages east of Vlasenica all the way to Kamenica on the Drina. So this is just an abridged view. So these were Serb areas that were taken by Muslims and they had to be returned to their rightful owners. That is the essence of the answer. That's it. I did not list 50 villages here now from the Drina all the way to Srebrenica and to Drinjaca. That is 80 kilometres. I just said what the central place was. And please note that it says here that the road should be repaired. Milici, Konjevic Polje, Zvornik, please, where is all of that. This road is a vital road and it led to the Alumina factory, from the bauxite mines to the Alumina factory, so the road should be kept running. And on both sides of that road, there are Muslim areas, Serb areas, in particular when one knows for sure, as is the case, that the drivers who were driving the ore were killed in Konjevic Polje, as drivers, not as soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Are you saying in a nutshell that the -- that the removal of Muslim civilians from these areas was justified because you wanted to replace them with Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to protect them that so that they would not lose their lives. That is my answer. To protect them so that they would not lose their lives. And you will save them if you keep them far away from the front line because even the innocent get killed at the front.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Did you need to burn the houses from which you -- in the villages that you attacked?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Which houses?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You were burning homes, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please. These are very harsh words, too harsh. These are not houses. These are points of resistance of the enemy army, and from each and every window, I repeat from each and every window there were machine-guns that were firing and then also there were observers who guided the fire. So these are strongholds, combat strongholds. Why did I not burn Srebrenica? Or, for example, why did we not burn that settlement in Jadar that was used by the Muslims, that was put up by the United Nations? So I said when there was no resistance, there would be no torching. That's my answer. That's the truth. And that's why Srebrenica did stay on with all of its housing potential.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: We are not talking about Srebrenica yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can we look at P03162?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm just trying to understand your claim in your statement at paragraph 15. You said it was the right and the duty of the Drina Corps to ensure the restitution of houses and land belonging to Serbian civilians. Yes? That's what you say in your statement. Looking here at an order --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Who else?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask whether the witness has a copy of his own statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm unable to assist. I don't know if he was provided with one. I'm showing him a document on the screen, D -- P03162.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: We could give him a hard copy, if you allow.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: That would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm trying to understand your evidence at paragraph 15. Perhaps you can just take a look at it. You can look at the last -- last sentence which is the sentence I just read out. Got it? Last sentence. I just read it out and I would like you to look at the document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what was it that you read out?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: The last sentence at paragraph 15.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the target of the attack was never Muslim civilians but only the Muslim forces who had massacred the Serb civilians. It was the right and the duty of the Drina Corps to ensure the restitution of houses and land belonging to Serbian civilians. Now, what is unclear here?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can you take a look, please, at this document, this report that you have on the screen. You can see here it's a report from Andric, then Lieutenant-Colonel Andric, 2nd of March. It's a report to the Drina Corps command, 2nd of March, 1993. Right? And I'd like you to look at the second paragraph, please, last sentence, and what he's reporting there, and I'll read it out, is: "The village of Gobelji has been burnt and tomorrow the plan is to do Paljevine." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your units were burning villages, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Wait a minute, wait a minute. Allow me to ask you something. Why will you not read the first paragraph out to me of this very same document? We should not just look at segments of documents and analyse them. We should look at the entirety of documents and analyse them. Please look at paragraph 1 of this document, look at what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm asking you about that last sentence and about that village. That's what I want to ask you about.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no. I cannot answer before you read out officially paragraph 1. Read out paragraph 1 and then we are going to see how come Andric's forces are in these mentioned areas. We have to take into account paragraph 1 as the first paragraph that relates to the developments themselves. Please read out the first paragraph, just as you've asked to have the other one read out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't understand your answer. This document is already in our evidence. You can read paragraph -- you can read paragraph, and if you would like, you can refer to paragraph 1. Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This has to do with a counterattack of a unit of the Birac Brigade commanded by Svetozar Andric. Obviously, these two mentioned villages were points of resistance of the enemy in combat operations. Certainly, that could not have been skipped, if you look at the terrain, if you look at the forces involved, and if you look at the task itself. I'm not justifying the burning of villages as villages, but if a village turns into a point of resistance, from which the enemy opens fire, then unfortunately that village had been abused by the same party that had turned the village into an enemy resistance point. So my answer is yes, and --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Let's go to --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know why you are interrupting me mid-sentence or mid-word. I said that the mentioned villages were not a priori supposed to be burned as such. It was the enemy that was supposed to be expelled from these villages, the enemy. I repeat: The enemy. It's not the people that were the enemy, nor will the people be the enemy, so that is what is stated here.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: What is stated here is that this village is burned. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, it was burned because that village was used for combat operations launched by the enemy. They chose to set up positions in the village. Why didn't they set up their positions in the mountains and why didn't they remove the population from the combat area --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Let's look --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This has to do with the clash of two armies, two units. This is not an attack of one army against an innocent village. Let us be clear on that. This is a clash of units in combat. And that clash is happening through villages, as you can see, and let us be clear on this. Many villages would be abused, as such, and would suffer terrible damage and nobody is denying that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Let's go to P03161, please, 03161. In the B/C/S, please, can we go to the second page.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And on the second page there, it's the second paragraph I want you to look at. It talks about Gobelji. I'm going to read out the English, the bottom of the English. "In the course of the day, special units of the 1st Birac Light Infantry Brigade took and destroyed the village of Gobelji, thus freeing up the left flank of the main forces in the attack on Cerska. At the entry into the village, our soldiers found weapons and other military equipment, as well as food and cattle, which the enemy left behind when fleeing from our forces." They had left. The enemy had left, and then the village was burned; isn't that right? All the villagers had been forced out. And the village was empty.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean expelled, if groups of soldiers and weapons were found? Expelling is different in military jargon. That means that the other side is taking part in expulsions. However, here, you can see that what was found there were those who had turned the village into a combat position. There were people there, there was military equipment, ammunition, all sorts of things, as you can see. There is no population there. The population had been taken out of there. So it wasn't that we expelled the population. These are two different concepts.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: They didn't need to burn the village, did they?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, what was necessary and what was not necessary, that is debatable. They cannot pass through that for as long as there is resistance being put up in that area. This is a basic military rule. You cannot go through enemy lines with the enemy still firing at you. That's the point, not destroying houses. I felt that. It was my own experience that somebody tore down my own house, destroyed my own house. But the point is that fire should not be opened from houses as such. That's the point.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You, General, you ordered the burning and destruction of Muslim villages, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can we look at P --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- it was a response to their attack, their attack, described in paragraph 1 of this document and it's the same fight.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can we see P5261, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Now, this is an intercept dated the 8th of February, 1993, of a conversation between you and Gaborovic, that's Second Lieutenant Slobodan Gaborovic of the 5th Communications Battalion. You know him, yes?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember the man.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You talk about talking to a Captain Jevdjevic. That would be Milenko Jevdjevic, wouldn't it, commander -- commander of the 5th Communications Battalion; is that right? Remember him?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: This is a communication you had with Gaborovic on the 8th of February, 1993. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what I spoke about with whom. We have to look at what we talked about. If this coincides with the truth, I will say "yes," but I need to read the text first. If I'm allowed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm going to read you the bottom five lines just to remind you what you said.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's fair. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You can read it in B/C/S. You say: "Catch up with them and fuck their mothers now." Answer: "Understood" --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Stop, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Excuse me. Let me -- let me finish reading. Then you say: "Hold tightly the positions. Are the Turks' houses burning?" Answer: "They are burning, they are burning." Question: "Way to go. As many as possible." That's you, isn't it? That's you inciting your units to burn as many Muslim homes as possible; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please, my lady, this ugly word never slipped from my mouth, not even in a barroom, let alone in an official conversation. I could not have uttered such an ugly word. That's one. Two: That I incited units to accomplish the task set before them, of course I did. That's the main task of a commander. Not to commit crimes but to accomplish a mission. That's the point and that's my answer. And besides, these are signalsmen. This is not my conversation with the subordinate commander or the superior commander. This kind of slang does not hold water. That I did urge them to reach the lines they were supposed to reach, to accomplish the missions that were set, of course every commander on the planet would do the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: "Way to go. As many as possible." That's what you said, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What would make you happy, that I would have said as few as possible and you suffer as many losses as you can? Just find me one word where I said kill a civilian? You cannot find that because that would not be me. And the fact that I was a commander who was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, Ms. Pack didn't ask you whether you ordered to kill somebody. Her question was whether you ordered to burn the houses. Do you see the sentence where you said, you heard that they were burning, they were burning. You asked them: "Are the Turks' house burning?" Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that. Thank you. Your Honour, do I have to repeat 100 times that these houses were organised as enemy structures to fire at our forces? This was no longer a house. It was a multi-storey bunker. It's a different matter if you attack at an inhabited house where a family is inside. But if the owner has moved out and somebody else came and put up a machine-gun nest there, covered it with sandbags, that was no longer a house. That was an enemy structure. Unfortunately, that happened by and large.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Go to P04253, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: The consequence of all this burning, General, was you didn't have houses to put the Serbian population in once the Muslim population had left; that's right, isn't it? Let's look at this order. I apologise, it's a report. I'll repeat my question when you've had a look at this. It's a report from Commander Major Vinko Pandurevic. It's dated the 10th of March, 1993, and it recommends at the bottom of the English and B/C/S, the last sentence, it recommends this: "We propose that houses should not be torched when taking control of Konjevic Polje, but that they be inhabited by people from Tuzla and other areas." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Now, he's suggesting, isn't he, that his brigade stop burning houses so that they can be inhabited by Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In this area, because Konjevic Polje is in a valley, in a depression, there was no fighting, there was no resistance. That's the point, because Konjevic Polje was not being defended by any forces. It's simply not a defence position. And it's logical that the enemy command realised they would unnecessarily only suffer losses there, that it was no use to put up their defences there. They put them up instead four or five kilometres away. And it was the same as in Srebrenica. And of course as long as houses were not turned into bunkers, there was no enemy fire coming from there, et cetera, the houses were not torched. And it's true that there were so many homeless people at the same time, and suddenly you get 15, 20 intact houses that were never in a combat zone. The houses, I repeat, were never burned unless there was a military purpose to it, unless they were used for enemy activity.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: That's not the case, is it, General? "Are the Turks' houses burning?" Your units had been deliberately burning villages, hadn't they, deliberately burning villages, pursuant to your orders; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I repeat for the umpteenth time: No orders were given to torch houses. Instead, as you noticed yourself, there were enemy soldiers inside those houses, enemy weapons, enemy equipment. And if we are talking about houses, just remember my house, shown on the screen recently. Those were innocent people. What we are talking about here is a conflict between warring parties. I repeat for the umpteenth time: Why was not Srebrenica burned? Why were no other places burned? Because there was no conflict there. There was no torching.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I want to look at the various means by which you sought to force the civilian population out of the Podrinje. Wasn't just through attacking, burning their villages, was it? You restricted the passage of humanitarian aid; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I expected you to read that I was proposed for commendation and, indeed, was commended by those people who were responsible for transport of humanitarian aid, instead of being blamed for restricting it. That is completely inaccurate. The accused here today, Mr. Karadzic, urged and insisted, time and time again, that humanitarian aid be transported to Srebrenica even at the very high cost to us that was paid. In November 1992, Karadzic ordered me to escort a humanitarian convoy through Bratunac. I had a very, very hard time convincing the people in Bratunac that the convoy has to be allowed to pass to the Muslim population in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And I was in a great deal of trouble and even my life was at risk in that operation because I was in danger from all sorts of militaries and non-militaries.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'd like to bring up, please, 65 ter 01201. It's a -- would have to be admitted under seal, so I would ask that it is even not shown on the public screens or that we go into private session while we are looking at this. In fact, we will have to go into private session while we are talking about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, it's 65 ter 09194. Now, this is an update by UNHCR, the UN High Commission for Refugees.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And again, I'm afraid, General, it's in English. I'm going to read the bottom three paragraphs to you: "Despite daily attempts by UNHCR to reach the eastern enclaves, no convoy has been allowed to deliver aid to the town of Gorazde" --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: If I can just read the bottom three paragraphs: "Despite daily attempts by UNHCR to reach the eastern enclaves, no convoy has been allowed to deliver aid to the town of Gorazde since the 19th of January. No food has reached Zepa since the 17th of January, and all convoys into Srebrenica have been banned since the 10th December 1992. UNHCR has been denied any access at all into the Cerska/Kamenica area, although Serb forces temporarily opened a one-way humanitarian corridor allowing people to leave but no aid to enter. "Nearly 5.000 people have already been forced to flee to Tuzla, mostly in extremely bad condition, some losing their fingers and toes due to frostbite. UNHCR has received unconfirmed reports of another 5.000 people in Srebrenica waiting to come out."

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: These were -- this was the sort of international condemnation of which you were aware; right? Condemnation of the blocking of humanitarian aid to these areas.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This level of document would not reach my level of command. I repeat again: We never obstructed any orders issued by the superior command. We have to make that clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You created the one way humanitarian corridor, didn't you, in the Cerska/Kamenica area?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, absolutely not. Please, I had a superior command. Do not try to portray me as an independent commander who has no superiors, no subordinates, who is working without directives, without orders. The word "subordination" is the key to the work of all military units, in peacetime and especially in wartime. God forbid that I should have obstructed anything or prevented any convoys from entering Srebrenica. I put my life at risk so that convoys could reach Srebrenica. Ask convoy leaders with whom they had the closest cooperation at that time. From 1992, when I was still covered in bandages and suffered from deep wounds, with whom did they work best? Always, I repeat always, I was in favour of helping the population, aiding the population. And please don't try to paint me as this person who prevented convoys from passing through despite orders being given to the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I asked you about this particular corridor that they are talking about, the one-way humanitarian corridor in Cerska/Kamenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And before I go on to my next question, I'd ask to admit this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6480, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm grateful. Just before we leave this topic, I'd like to look, please, at 65 ter 09379.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You controlled access to these areas that you were attacking, didn't you? Yes?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On orders, on orders, nothing at my own initiative, with a clear report provided on what was done according to the orders. Not taking anything from the convoys. Never making people's work difficult. But inspecting the convoys, of course, that was according to the orders we received. People had to check the trucks and that did not come from me. I did not make that up. Nor did my superior or subordinate commander, for that matter, make that up. But that we did invest huge efforts for these convoys to reach the Muslim population, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: That's right. So you acted under orders, is that what you're saying? Is that your evidence? On the topic of blocking humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I repeat, because we had to inspect the contents, not that we would not allow the convoy to reach the Muslims. These are two different things. You have to look at the contents of the order sent from the top down to us subordinates. You have to see it as a whole. They never said that we should take the convoy prisoners or the people who were in it. Not a word about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Let's just look at this particular corridor that was set up, this one-way corridor that was set up and is described in this document, one of your combat reports dated the 1st of February, 1993. And if we just look at the bottom of the page in the English and at page 2, please, in the B/C/S, we are looking at paragraph 3, describing the situation on the territory of the AOR: "The Ustasha leaders have felt that their inhabitants shall move out of Cerska/Srebrenica area and stop being their hostages. I decided to allow the inhabitants to move the same way and itinerary as previously tomorrow," and so on. And then you say: "It shall be possible to leave the territory for all people without exception and only with my permission." And this is a document that is -- comes from you, doesn't it, the Drina Corps command, and it's signed by you; is that right? And this is a -- that was nodding your head [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And this is a corridor controlled by you through which your denying humanitarian aid access; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, that's not right. The convoy is being protected and why? Because this route was threatened by infiltrated elements. God knows which. There were all kinds. They infiltrated. Those were such times, a paramilitary formation, the Muslim or the Serbian one, could block a truck, take the driver prisoner and take away the whole truck, and I was responsible for the route. Why until this hour? Because it was getting dark, and during the night such a convoy could not be allowed to move because that would really be shallow way of commanding on my part, if I was to allow the convoy to travel along such a route regardless of what might befall it. It could even be destroyed en route. So how could one justify that? There were no longer any conditions for such an action to be carried out and the superior gentlemen, I mean my own superior command and the civilian commands and the UNPROFOR and all the other institutions, I have them all in mind, they would have to provide the guarantees so as to make this travel safe for the convoy. That's the essence of the story, because you cannot let a convoy travel during the night. Come on, people. Even the lights do not allow a vehicle to move because the light is red and not green, and let alone if you have rifles and the conditions of war and it's night time. You have to realise all that because you keep reminding me of the situation. You're putting me back into the position where it's not as if you just pressed a button and allowed the convoy to pass or not. But what we managed to achieve was that the people in the convoy were alive and well, the contents of the convoy were transported to the address, and it was late but the superior command or God knows who else who was above us ordered that it had to be inspected. I had my men who inspected it. There was a report about what was being transported. So don't criticise us by saying we did not allow the convoy to pass. We needed to create the conditions for the convoy to move safely. And after this hour, look at the calendar, look at the dates, night would fall, and the terrain was treacherous. So it wasn't just like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Pause, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'd like admit that document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: We're going to move to 1994 --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6481, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I want to look further at the task you were implementing, the task under directive 4 that were you implementing, the task to create conditions to force the Muslim population out of the Podrinje area. That task. 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can we look at P04075, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Now you can see on the screen this is a report from Slavko Ognjenovic, who then was the commander of the Bratunac Brigade. It's dated 4th July 1994, and I want you, please, to look at paragraph 1. He is writing this report, as you can see, for his brigade following a briefing at the Drina Corps, the Drina Corps command, in Vlasenica, and this was a briefing that was attended by Mladic. Now, you, General, you, Ognjenovic and other Drina Corps brigade commanders, you were all present at that meeting on the 1st July 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's probably so. If the memo is signed, then it's certainly so.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You'd agree you were at the meeting. Let's just see what Ognjenovic says. Consequent upon it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Page 2 in the English, please, and 2 in the B/C/S. It's 2 going to 3 quite soon in the English and 2 in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Now, this is the report being written as a result of that meeting. And it says: "We have won the war in Podrinje but we have not beaten the Muslims completely, which is what we must do in the next period. We must attain our final goal, an entirely Serbian Podrinje. The enclaves of Srebrenica, Zepa and Gorazde must be defeated militarily. We must continue to arm, train, discipline, and prepare the RS army for the execution of this crucial task, the expulsion of Muslims from the Srebrenica enclave. There will be no retreat when it comes to the Srebrenica enclave. We must advance. The enemy's life has to be made unbearable and their temporary stay in the enclave impossible so that they leave the enclave en masse as soon as possible, realising that they cannot survive there." Now, Ognjenovic there is repeating the order, isn't he, which Mladic gave at the briefing which you attended in Vlasenica on the 1st of July; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But it's not quite as you just read it out. You passed lightly over the place where he says that they have to be defeated militarily. Defeated militarily. We were warring parties. Or a third side at Dayton, which I believe should have been organised in 1992 rather than 1995, where somebody else tells us: Stop, the war is over and now the judge begins to judge. However, it says here defeated militarily. And as Ognjenovic -- let me paint the picture for you. As Ognjenovic was politically educated, he allowed himself a lot of epic sweep in his report, and eventually that was why he was removed from his position in that brigade. Don't use that against me. I don't think it's necessary for me to analyse Ognjenovic. But it's logical while you are at war, and as long as someone is shooting at you, or threatening to launch an attack on you, you will make efforts to try and prevent that. You know quite well that at this time the ostensibly protected enclave was growing to the size of a division, and a division, as a notion in the army, denotes something huge. And that was created in a protected enclave. You should have also read out to me what weaponry the Muslim side was requesting from Tuzla, so it would be easier for you to read out to me what you have. They requested so much weapons that they would have been able to kill everybody all the way up to Belgrade. There are documents testifying to that. Let us not extract things from documents like you extract teeth from somebody's jaws. There was a latent danger for us to disappear officially when the 28th Division was to launch an attack against our positions, together with Gorazde, together with Sarajevo, together with Zepa, together with Tuzla, and what was I supposed to do? To let them to kill us all to the last one? I don't know who you would be asking these questions then. Thank you. That was the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: What -- I'm not clear what your answer is. The enemy's life has to be made unbearable and their temporary stay in the enclave impossible so that they leave the enclave en masse as soon as possible, realising that they cannot survive there. I've got to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Now, that was the order that Mladic gave on the 1st July at the briefing in Vlasenica; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Look, this is not an order. Please. It's not an order. The order begins under item 4, where he says: I have decided. Everything else is just talks, agreements, preparations for orders and so on. An order has its framework. It has its whole. It has its contents and clear instructions stating who should be doing what. That's an order.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your aim was to create conditions for the enclaves to disappear; right? That was your aim.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And was the aim for anything Serbian to disappear in Podrinje, the aim of the enemy side? Wasn't that the aim of the enemy side, that everything that was Serbian in Podrinje should vanish? Or did they have some other aim? Please, let us be human. Was the aim -- I'll repeat for the third time, was the aim of the enemy side that everything that is Serbian should disappear from Podrinje? That was their aim. Our aim was to survive, and we have survived. And they are survived too.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your aim was to make life unbearable for them, unbearable so they couldn't survive, so they would have to leave; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they have destroyed my life and I preserved theirs. Will you understand that we could have destroyed these lives with our weapons? If we were some sort of butchers, we could have destroyed, cut off their lives as they destroyed mine. Did they leave anyone alive?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You wrote a diary as commander of the Drina Corps, didn't you, and that diary was seized from your home in October 2009 and is now in possession of the Office of the Prosecutor? That's right, it was seized from your home, you remember that, in October 2009?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I remember. I remember a very unpleasant -- not 2009. It was the 16th of July, 2010. I suppose I know when they attacked me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It was seized by the MUP. And I'm going to ask you now to look at the diary for 1994, which is 65 ter 21899A, please. I'm going to ask you to look at an extract from one of your diaries, notebooks. This is the extract for the 1 July 1994 meeting with Mladic and Ognjenovic.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.
