utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You recognise it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Only you didn't let me say in what way this personal document of mine reached you. You should have allowed me to clarify that in half a minute.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about this entry on the 1st July 1994. I'd like you to take a look at it, please. You'd agree these are the notes of your briefing at the Drina Corps in Vlasenica? Yes? The command?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You made those notes at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, just like any officer keeps notes. That was how I kept mine.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask to ask the witness to read it out aloud because it's not well translated. It's not a great error, it's not crucial, but it's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The penultimate sentence above the eyes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to take the witness to various sections of it. It will take a while to go through the whole lot, so we can leave the first page.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Just to note that this is General Mladic talking, right? Where you see his name there, you're noting down what he says? Yes? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- you can read -- perhaps just read what --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Should I read it? May I?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead. Read what he says under what he says.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Keep your eyes peeled, what does that mean? Literally it's keep your six eyes open because a --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can you pause there --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- man has two eyes, you should keep vigilant because the danger is great.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Pause, please. What we don't want it is to have you interpreting what was said because we are just trying to see what is written on the page. It may be that I should read it in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Now, let's go to the following page, please, at page 2. I'm going to read that in English. It continues to be what Mladic is saying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Pack --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you didn't let me -- you didn't allow --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- could you take note of what the reporter was saying? Shall we continue? The question will be coming, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm going to read slowly from this: "Keynote address and guidelines for reporting. Report openly and as it is. I won't praise you too much. You did a lot. We are on our way to clean the enclaves."

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You noted there what Mladic said to you at the briefing in Vlasenica on the 1st July. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And let us go, please, to the following page. I'm going to keep to the notes of what Mladic has said. There is a note in a box at the bottom of the page: "General Mladic, do not let the convoys pass to Tuzla for the time being." That's another note of what Mladic said, yes?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And the following page --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May I explain this? May I clarify it?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: We'll deal with it at the end. I'm just going to go through the entry.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Page 4, please, just so we get the order. I'm not going to read this out. More from Mladic, Krstic, Mladic again. And to the following page, 5, please. "Mladic: Detailed control of convoys. Fight even with UNPROFOR. Cut through the area" --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't see it. I can't see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: My apologies, let's just take it up. It's halfway down the page under the -- looks like it's under the line that you've drawn. And you can see Mladic --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Just to take it up: "Cut through the area around the road." And then the next bit we can go over as I'm reading: "The enclave is not to survive but to disappear."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Objection. It is absolutely unacceptable for the Defence to make this sort of salad of words. It's not to "cut" but "cut through." It means to cut the forest. Nothing is translated correctly. And especially so many words are listed --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object -- I object to this sort of intervention [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I request that the witness be allowed to respond to a single sentence each time and not such a selection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, she is asking -- she has come to the passage where it says: "The enclave is not to survive but to disappear." I think she was coming to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Yes. And let's just continue one further extract and then I'm done with reading. You can see Ognjenovic, there is a line, perhaps he says something, then we have Mladic again. "The enclaves are air landing facilities. The war has not even started, let alone that it has completed. Reduce the enclave," and so it goes on. And that's the end of my reading of that portion of this entry although I will be taking it up further in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: So let's just pause at this language that you note down, that Mladic uses: "We are on the way to clean the enclave. The enclave is not to survive but to disappear." My question to you, General, this was your preoccupation in the Drina Corps, wasn't it, creating conditions so that the civilian population would leave, by this time leave the enclaves; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was much better for him to go to the areas outside of the combat zone than to be within such a zone where there were no conditions for life because Srebrenica was too crowded with refugees who had gone there after our offensive in the spring 1993. They did not accept a peaceful solution. I offered it and I wanted to tell you about it here today but you cut me off. And you must notice here that it says that those protected enclaves are turning into areas for launching air raids. So the elementary knowledge of us soldiers would imply we know quite well what an air raid area means, and having in mind that in the same area powerful military formations were being prepared, I don't know what a command in a situation of war would say then not to allow the creation for air raids from such an area. It shouldn't be allowed to be used for that. And the population such as the Serbian population would flee to Serbia and wherever they were fortunate enough to escape. So what was meant here was that their population should simply leave the area, which was very unfavourable for life. That's what it was. They did not have a single hectare of arable land. Not a single factory was operational. I personally made efforts for them to get water. Why don't you read out that sentence to me? I did that personally, myself. I made sure that people had water. Because I know quite well how much and what exactly that means. And to have people around yourself as a sort of mask and keep setting up a division all the while, somehow I cannot take that indifferently. Yes, people should be removed, always. Why not? Remove the civilian population from the area where war is being waged. That's the most painless thing. The idea is not that the population should be removed in the way that it should be killed, no, not that, not that, but that they would be saved. And that's the end of my answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: So this is what you say, what was meant here was that - let me just repeat your words - "the population should simply leave the area, which was very unfavourable for life." It was unfavourable for life, General, wasn't it, because of the conditions created by you. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean we created it? You forgot the map that we showed at the beginning of my testimony here. How can you say that? What about the 157 torched Serbian villages? You are too clever to forget this so fast. Where are theses villages? Please, sit in a helicopter and make a tour of this area and you can find the burned foundations of these villages where life is not continuing as it was even to this day. That's the substance.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we continue tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of the time. Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, I just have to add one sentence. We never come to say that an armed formation of the 28th Muslim Division used their own people as a mask for tears and I don't know what. I'm not -- I haven't managed to achieve that all Serbs would return to their destroyed villages to this day, 20 years later, let alone having all these people pushed into an enclave and then have a big problem. It seemed to be a problem to everyone except for the Muslim armed formations. That's what it was. Do you know that personally they wrote to me in the midst of the war and beseeched me to come and command them and come to save them? Why don't you read such a letter to me? You do have it. You do. Finished.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, you said you kept that map in your office. Did you hang that on the wall of your office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, on the wall. Your Honours, on the wall. On the wall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So what's the point of hanging that map on your wall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because of the circles, the squares, the rectangles, the rhomboids, the intentions of the enemy command were discovered, the axis of attack, taking of vital facilities, economic and topographic ones, because there was always a threat, a danger that the hydroelectric power plant at Bajina Basta would be destroyed and that a lake of poisoned water from zinc and lead mines in Sase would also be destroyed, where fish all the way to the Black Sea would be exterminated. So these were the vital facilities that we had to save.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Pack, unless you have some urgent matters, shall we adjourn here?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes. Would you prefer, Mr. President, to deal with the question of admission of this extract tomorrow? Simply I would be asking for admission but perhaps tomorrow --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There should be no opposition. We will admit it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6482, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we adjourn today the Chamber will issue an oral ruling on the Prosecution motion to exclude in part evidence of Witness Miroslav Toholj filed on 22nd October 2013, as well as on the Prosecution request for leave to reply to Karadzic's response filed on the 29th of October, 2013. The Prosecution requests that a number of paragraphs be excluded from the statement of Miroslav Toholj sought to be tendered pursuant to Rule 92 ter on the basis that they are irrelevant to the charges in the indictment. The accused filed his response on the 28th of October opposing the motion. The Chamber has reviewed the submissions and examined the statement. It is of the view that paragraphs 5, 6, 7, 8, 13, 14, 15, 18, 21, the first two sentences of paragraph 27, paragraphs 32, 35, 46, 47, the last two sentence of paragraph 56, paragraphs 57, 58, 59 in its entirety, 68, 69 and 70 should be excluded as they go into the detail of areas not relevant to the charges in the indictment. However, the Chamber is of the view that paragraphs 11, 12, 19, and 20, may remain as they may be of some relevance. The Chamber therefore grants the motion in part, orders the exclusion of the paragraphs identified earlier, including, proprio motu, the exclusion of paragraph 59 in its entirety, allows the accused to tender the remainder of Toholj's statement pursuant to Rule 92 ter and denies the Prosecution request for leave to reply. Mr. Zivanovic, we will adjourn for today and continue tomorrow morning at 9.00. I'd like to advise you not to discuss with anybody else about your testimony while you are giving your evidence here at the Tribunal. Hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you for your advice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 31st day of October, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.49 p.m.,
